name: Doctiq
cap: the ultimate workspace for modern clinics
note: PRD to shipped product in 2 weeks ;)
title: Designing an AI-powered clinic SaaS app, shipped in two weeks
sub: Overhauled Doctiq's core platform into a hands-free, AI-driven clinic and hospital workspace, ahead of a regional medical expo.
snapshot: Doctiq is an AI-powered operating system for clinics and hospitals. As founding product designer, I was tasked with overhauling the core platform and shipping a cohesive, demo-ready product in two weeks, ahead of a major regional medical expo. Working solo with an AI-augmented workflow, I designed a hands-free clinical workspace built around ambient voice scribing, automated WhatsApp patient triage and deep modularity.
metrics: qualified leads at the medical expo
problem_intro: Traditional electronic medical record (EMR) platforms in India force clinicians to spend more time typing into rigid forms than engaging with patients. Four problems compounded:
problems: Doctors spend up to 40% of a consultation manually typing symptoms, vitals and medication instructions.
Inefficient handling of WhatsApp inquiries meant high drop-off, empty slots and revenue leakage.
Incumbents (Practo, DocOn, Eka Care, KiviHealth) impose fixed data schemas that can't flex to multi-specialty workflows, wards or custom prescriptions.
Senior doctors and hospital directors routinely abandon clinical software with steep learning curves.
problem_close: the brief was as much constraint as problem: solve all of this, cohesively, in two weeks.
goals_b: Move clinics from fragmented admin software to an automated, hands-free workspace
Differentiate from rigid incumbents through automation and deep customization
goals_u: Give clinicians back their time by removing manual documentation
Reduce front-desk bottlenecks and missed patient inquiries
Make the platform usable by non-technical staff with almost no learning curve
goals_img_alt: Clinic automation goals: automation, customization, time savings, efficiency, usability
users_img_alt: Healthcare software adoption: the pain points clinics told us about
users_intro: Despite the compressed timeline, I grounded the work in real discovery:
methods: Deconstructed Practo, DocOn, Eka Care and KiviHealth: crowded navigation, no hands-free input, rigid billing.
In-depth interviews with 4 practicing doctors to observe real consultation patterns and pain points.
Rapid sessions with the founder and lead engineer to turn business concepts into user flows.
personas: "Dr. Traditional". Needs zero-friction documentation that removes typing without cluttering the consultation room.
Needs live visibility into patient queues, inventory dispensing and automated message triage.
Needs real-time bed occupancy, multi-department admissions and unified billing.
insight: For non-technical clinicians, the winning move wasn't more features. It was getting the interface out of the way: the less the software asked doctors to do, the more they'd trust and adopt it.
principles: Hands-free first
Favor voice and automation over forms; every removed keystroke is a win.
Speak human, not software
Name features for what they do: Voice-to-Prescription, not "NLP".
Clarity for the non-technical
Senior doctors and directors must get productive fast, without training.
Surface what matters
Auto-populate the essentials; tuck raw complexity into drawers.
Modular by design
Let clinics customize without breaking backend data integrity.
solution_intro: I designed Doctiq as a clinical workspace. The headline features:
features: An ambient scribe turns multi-language consultations (English, Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi, Bengali) into editable vitals, symptoms, diagnoses and medications.
A two-pane console that automates WhatsApp inquiries and booking, with instant AI Mode / Human Mode overrides.
A bed-status matrix with admissions, active charts and charge ledgers, closing the discharge payment-leakage gap.
Cohort selection with a live, device-accurate preview, sent asynchronously so campaigns never slow the clinic.
Progress bars and quest cards that reward staff with credits and badges, speeding up daily adoption.
A toggle from clinical light mode to a slate dark canvas, cutting glare across long shifts.

imgs.alt: AI inbox: WhatsApp conversations with patients

Milestones: quest board and reward feed

impact_img_alt: Impact of the medical expo and the AI receptionist
trade_note: the interesting calls were about restraint.
tradeoffs: Stored the raw transcription in a collapsible drawer and gave the main interface to auto-populated prescription fields.
the doctor sees decisions, not noise.
Built a modular Template Configuration Engine for letterheads, custom fields and reports, without breaking backend validation.
Prioritized an agile token architecture over a full component library, refining components in code alongside the developer.
shipped on deadline, with tokens that still scale.
impact: qualified leads captured at the medical expo through live demos
clinics and a multi-specialty hospital deployed, 2 more in rollout
less administrative documentation overhead in piloted practices
more after-hours bookings through the 24/7 AI receptionist
for non-technical staff to reach proficiency, with no formal training
reflection: Designing for healthcare is an exercise in subtraction. The wins came from stripping away jargon and keystrokes, not adding features.

AI, used deliberately, changes what a solo designer can ship: I planned, tested and delivered an enterprise-grade product in two weeks without handing over a single strategic decision. Renaming a technical NLP feature to "Voice-to-Prescription" did as much for adoption as any screen. Next, I'd formalize the token foundation into a full design system now that the product has proven itself.
setup: 2-week high-velocity redesign sprint, ahead of a regional medical expo
Gemini → Claude Design → JSON design tokens → Figma foundation → handover

name: Speak+
kicker: Case study 02 · EdTech · Wall Street English
title: Reviving a dead app: from 5 to 2,000+ paying users in 6 months
sub: Repositioning a failing standalone EdTech app into a core product feature, driving 2,000+ paid subscriptions through UX strategy and ecosystem integration.
snapshot: Speak+ was a standalone English-speaking-practice app that had stalled at 5 paying users: decent downloads, almost no conversion. Rather than pour budget into acquiring new users, I repositioned Speak+ as a feature inside Wall Street English's trusted Core Course ecosystem, redesigning its positioning, onboarding and in-app promotion. In six months, paid subscriptions grew from 5 to 2,000+.
problem_intro: Wall Street English is a global English-learning company built on structured courses and speaking practice with real teachers. Speak+ began as a separate B2C app: unlimited small-group speaking classes on a monthly subscription. On paper it worked. In practice it was dying.
problems: As a standalone product, Speak+ sat outside any structured learning journey, so new users couldn't see why it mattered.
Little to build trust meant free trials rarely converted.
problem_close: a strong feature, trapped in the wrong container: a standalone app.
goals_b: Grow paid Speak+ subscriptions by integrating it into the ecosystem, not acquiring users externally
Extend recurring revenue by keeping students engaged beyond course completion
Reduce dependency on costly external B2C acquisition
goals_u: Give advanced learners a clear way to keep improving after structured courses
Make Speak+'s value obvious within the learning journey
Offer flexible, unlimited practice tied to real-life communication
users_intro: The people most likely to convert were already inside the ecosystem: existing Core Course students, a warm and trusting audience who simply weren't upgrading.
methods: Asked learners what they valued and where Speak+ fit (or didn't) in their week.
Looked at where students dropped off and where upgrade prompts were ignored.
Teachers were already recommending Speak+, and it still saw almost no adoption.
personas: Already paying for a structured course; doesn't want to pay twice for practice.
Finishing levels and looking for a way to keep speaking regularly.
Completed the course; at risk of drifting away without a reason to return.
insight: The barrier was never awareness or trust. Speak+ was built and priced as a separate product stacked on a course students had already paid for. It wasn't an acquisition gap. It was positioning, placement and pricing.
principles: Seamless
Integrated, not intrusive. Speak+ should feel like a continuation, not an upsell.
Valuable
Practice with purpose. Frame it as an essential fluency builder.
Trust-led
Promote without pressure. Contextual education, not aggressive upselling.
Scalable
Designed for growth. Reusable promotion surfaces and flexible entry points.
principles_img_alt: Speak+ strategic tenets: seamless, valuable, trust-led, scalable
solution_img_alt: Speak+ integration into the Core app, step by step
solution_intro: We repositioned Speak+ from a standalone app into a speaking-practice feature embedded directly inside the Core Course experience. Three moves carried the work:
features: Practice-first messaging and flows that framed Speak+ as the natural next step for advanced learners and alumni.
Contextual, milestone-based prompts across the dashboard, onboarding and level results, right when its value was clearest.
Embedded into existing subscriptions and alumni flows, so upgrading felt like continuing the journey.
screens_note: before and after: standalone Speak+ vs Speak+ in Core

imgs.alt: Before: Speak+ as a standalone app
After: Speak+ promoted inside the Core dashboard (some details blurred under NDA)

trade_note: the interesting decisions were about restraint, not features.
tradeoffs: Keeping Speak+ separate would preserve its identity; folding it into Core would cost that visibility. I chose integration.
faster adoption and revenue, at the cost of a standalone brand.
I prioritized integration and in-app promotion over new features.
significant growth, while feature work waited.
An aggressive upsell would convert faster short-term. I chose subtle, context-based education.
impact: revenue stream, instead of a failing standalone product
adoption grew among students and teachers
advanced learners stayed engaged with flexible, unlimited practice
reflection: A stalling product rarely needs more. It needs to be in the right place, at the right price.

Speak+ didn't fail because the practice was weak; it failed because it was framed as a separate purchase instead of a continuation of a journey students already trusted. The fix was distribution and positioning, not features. Next time I'd instrument the promotion surfaces from the start, to see which moment (onboarding, a level-up, course completion) actually drove upgrades.
setup: 2 months to integrate into the Core app · 5 months to promote and onboard franchises and users

name: Swimingo
title: Building trust into a two-sided swimming marketplace
sub: Redesigned Swimingo from a low-visibility listings site into a trust-first marketplace connecting swim instructors and learners.
snapshot: Swimingo is a two-sided marketplace connecting swimming instructors with learners: discovery, booking and progress tracking in one place. The early product was little more than a listings page. Instructors couldn't get visibility, customers couldn't find trusted instructors, and neither side had a reason to stay. I redesigned it into a structured, trust-first platform and led its rebrand from SwimNGo to Swimingo.
problem_intro: Swimingo set out to connect swimming instructors with learners, but the original product wasn't bridging the two sides.
problems: Instructors struggled to get visibility and manage their availability.
Customers couldn't easily discover verified instructors on schedules that fit.
No reliable, centralized platform: no standard for trust, no structure to bring either side back.
problem_close: in a two-sided marketplace, if neither side sees value, neither side stays.
goals_b: Increase instructor sign-ups and active listings
Improve retention and repeat bookings to drive revenue
Establish Swimingo as a trusted brand in the swimming-lesson market
goals_u: Help customers easily find safe, verified instructors
Let instructors manage schedules and bookings with ease
A smooth booking experience with clear communication and visible progress
users_intro: A two-sided marketplace has two customers with different goals, so I researched both, through competitor analysis and secondary research.
methods: Visibility, steady bookings and credibility, held back by poor coordination and clunky scheduling.
Safety, verified instructors, flexible schedules and small classes with clear pricing and progress.
personas: Wants flexible scheduling and, above all, safety for her child.
Seeks self-improvement and visible progress tracking.
Needs a structured program that works for diverse learners.
insight: In this market, trust is the currency. Not price, not features. Parents valued safety over cost, and instructors needed visible credibility before they'd commit.
principles: Trust-first
Every surface should earn confidence: verification, reviews, clarity.
Clarity over complexity
Two-sided doesn't have to mean complicated.
Minimize booking friction
The fewer steps to a booking, the better.
Personalize where it counts
Tailor to each side without over-engineering.
Structured but friendly
Organised enough to trust, warm enough to enjoy.
Conversion-focused onboarding
Onboarding is where trust, and retention, is won.
solution_intro: I rebuilt Swimingo into a structured two-sided platform, designed around trust and built to bring both sides back.
features: Availability that works for both sides.
Verification and trust built in from the first screen.
Tailored experiences for instructors and customers.
Visible improvement that keeps learners engaged.
solution_img_alt: Enhancing Swimingo's platform: the six features stacked
screens_note: the new Swimingo, after the rebrand

imgs.alt: Booking flow: from finding an instructor to a confirmed lesson
Swimingo landing page: learning how to swim, made easy

trade_img_alt: How to balance early exploration and long-term consistency
tradeoffs: Rather than build a full design system upfront, I prototyped the product and aligned components with stakeholder feedback as I went.
faster iteration, still building toward consistency.
I prioritized the moments that mattered most to each side, from one consistent system.
equal value to both sides, without doubling the complexity.
impact: increase in user retention, by month 3 of the revamp
social media engagement, paired with the rebrand
reflection: The hardest part of a marketplace isn't the interface. It's balance.

Every decision had to serve instructors and customers without tipping the experience toward either. Treating trust as the core design problem, not a nice-to-have, is what made it work: once both sides felt safe, engagement followed. Next, I'd invest earlier in a proper design system.
setup: Product & Brand Designer (sole designer). Led the rebrand from SwimNGo to Swimingo
